Autonomous science systems are usually evaluated on curated, hand-built micro-benchmarks: a synthetic dataset, a metric, a leaderboard. The hard part of real research — "can you actually beat the method the humans published?" — is almost never posed as a task. **Scientist World** (Princeton, with ai-scientist.world) closes that gap by making the literature itself the test suite.

An autonomous pipeline selects papers from arXiv's core AI categories (124,816 unique papers over fourteen months, screened down to 21,354 empirical-method candidates), extracts each paper's open-ended research question, and **reproduces the authors' proposed method as the baseline inside a working environment**. An AI-Scientist entering that environment is scored against what the human authors actually achieved — not against a toy target. The first release contains **1,000 verified environments**.

## Two Different Research Abilities

Evaluation runs in two modes: *improve* (the model receives the reproduced source method and must beat it) and *innovate* (no source code; design a method from scratch). The leaderboards split cleanly, which is the paper's more interesting claim. Fable 5 is strongest at improving existing work; Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 take the top two slots at inventing from scratch. Among open models, **GLM 5.2 places third at innovating**. The two abilities are only loosely correlated, so "does research" is not one skill.

The headline number: AI-Scientists **beat the paper's reproduced method in 84% of improve attempts and 74% of innovate attempts**. That is the fraction where the machine is ahead of the humans who wrote the paper.

## Effort Does Not Explain It

A tempting alternative explanation is that bigger budgets simply win. The authors check: **compute hours and agent turns explain essentially none of the score variance (R² ≤ 0.02)**. What does explain it is research quality. An LLM judge, blind to scores, rates each attempt on creativity, engineering, rigor, significance and depth — those ratings track the actual scores at **ρ = 0.89**. The winners are not the ones trying hardest; they are the ones doing better research.

## A Small Model Raised In The World

The same 1,000 environments double as a training ground. Each attempt is stored as a version-controlled repo with full trajectories, averaging 3.7 idea revisions, 6 method revisions, 25 experiments and 35 commits — **6,400 hours of research traces** in total.

Qwen3-8B is trained on them in two stages: SFT on 1,000 cleaned examples, then off-policy GRPO on 1,500 scored ideas. Ideation and implementation are separated, so a fixed frontier implementer (GPT 5.6 Sol) executes every idea identically and only the idea's origin varies. Median implemented idea score climbs **41 → 84 → 106 FNI**, a **+158%** gain that puts the small scientist's ideation at the frontier cohort's anchor.

The honest caveat: the 1,000 environments are a sample of *AI* papers with quantitative optimization contributions, not the whole of science, and the FNI metric normalizes heterogeneous scoring scales. Still, the framing shift is real — papers stop being documents and become playgrounds.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.08478](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08478)
